From Surat, the 21st February, Anno 1693. — Batavia. To his Excellency the Lord and Master Willem van Outhoorn and the Esteemed Excellencies, the Lords Councillors of Dutch India. Noble and Esteemed, Received on the 30th of the previous month, most manfully, well June 1643 per the ship the steadfastness, namely Gaspersdam, wise, foreseeing, very over Tuticorin and Coromandel. —. Generous Lords, Well Noble, High Commanding Lords. On the day of our departure from Malacca, I have, under the date of 17th January last, most humbly informed your High Excellencies; which letter, and the accompanying box with papers, I trust will have come into your Excellencies' hands; these few lines shall serve only to further inform your High Excellencies that our arrival at the roadstead of Colombo was on the 19th of this month, where we had previously learned that the lord governor of Ceylon had a fleet of eight ships at hand, and from Surat on the 21st February, Anno 1693. — frigates, to which two English ships had also joined themselves, which had been dispatched on the 14th of this month toward Malabar; wherefore, as it has been deemed good by the Ceylonese lord governor and council, your High Excellencies shall come to understand fully from their Excellencies' writing, wherefore I shall conduct myself most humbly in this regard, and shall only mention here that we, in order to advance our voyage and to hasten as much as lies in our power, and likewise in hope of catching up with the fleet at Malabar, today under God's gracious blessing intend to weigh anchor, the lord governor Thomas van Rhee having treated me with all courtesy, for which I am obliged to his Excellency, and I pray God that he may restore his Excellency to his former health, for the greatest service of the Esteemed Company; may that same God grant us a safe and speedy voyage, and preserve us from the haughty

--- CHUNK 4 ---
and likewise in hope of catching up with the fleet at Malabar, today under God's gracious blessing intend to weigh anchor, the lord governor Thomas van Rhee having treated me with all courtesy, for which I am obliged to his Excellency, and I pray God that he may restore his Excellency to his former health, for the greatest service of the Esteemed Company; may that same God grant us a safe and speedy voyage, and preserve us from the haughty and quarrelsome French enemy; but should we come to encounter him, I hope I shall conduct myself according to what is required of an honest man and faithful Company servant. With which, &c. (signed below) Well Noble, High Commanding Lords, Your Excellencies' Most Humble and Faithful Servant (was signed) Louis de Keyser. (in margin) Colombo, the 21st February, Anno 1693. — Register of Papers going from here per the fluyt Bovencaspel in the hands of the skipper Jan Tijssen van Buuren to be given at Tuticorin to the chief and from there sent via Ceylon to Batavia, consigned to his Excellency the lord and Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Excellencies, the Lords Councillors of Dutch India. --- CHUNK 2 ---
received on the 30th of June 1693 by the Yacht Gaasperdam via Coromandel. From Surat on the 14th of March in the year 1693. — Batavia. To His Excellency the Lord and Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Honorable Lords, Councilors of the Netherlands India, noble, earnest, highly esteemed, valiant, wise, prudent, most generous Lords. Most Noble, Highly Commanding Lords. On the 21st of February last past, having made ready to continue our journey from the roadstead of Colombo, I humbly reported this to Your Excellency under that date. Contrary winds and currents have delayed our fortunate journey, so that we did not reach Quilon before the 8th of this month after midnight, where we learned from the chief officer Sir Johannes Spilardus that the Lord Commander Isaac van Dielen would betake himself in person to the fleet, in order to observe the Company's interests northward at Wingurla and Surat on the 14th of March in the year 1693, in Canara, and to conduct the fleet as far as before Goa, where the four French ships that had been in Surat were staying; and since the chief of Quilon had not yet received any report of the Lord Commander's departure, I deemed it advisable to proceed myself to Cochin by small vessels — thinking whether the Lord Commander might still be there, so that I could meet with His Excellency and deliberate what should be undertaken for the greatest service of the Company; but upon arriving at Cochin I found that the Lord Commander had departed with the fleet on the 8th; concerning His Excellency's intentions, the administrator Vinck could give me no other information than that the Lord Commander had told him orally that he intended to proceed northward with the fleet as far as before Wingurla, and if the French should meet him on the way or before Goa, His Excellency would endeavor to ruin them,

--- CHUNK 3 ---
to be undertaken; but upon arriving at Cochin I found that the Lord Commander had departed with the fleet on the 8th; concerning His Excellency's intentions, the administrator Vinck could give me no other information than that the Lord Commander had told him orally that he intended to proceed northward with the fleet as far as before Wingurla, and if the French should meet him on the way or before Goa, His Excellency would endeavor to ruin them, or at the very least to drive them away. The fluyt Adriahem, meanwhile, had arrived at Cochin on the 12th of this month toward evening earlier than I had expected, having received more favorable winds than we had enjoyed some days before. The departure of the fleet (without hope of being able to overtake it due to the poor sailing qualities of the Adriahem), the four French ships at Goa, and the progress of the monsoon causing me concern, I requested the Honorable administrator Vinck to have the Cochin council convened and strengthened with the captains and chief pilots of the fluyt Adriahem and Bovencaspel, as well as the Cochin equipment master, which having been done, I presented to the combined council yesterday or on the 13th of this month whether it would be advisable to continue our journey notwithstanding that it is quite late in the monsoon, especially since the 4 French ships must be presumed still to be before Goa, as long as no certain news of their departure has been received; the defensive fleet could well avoid them, but would then betake itself again before Goa or come down along the Malabar Coast; whereby we, from Surat on the 14th of March in the year 1693, would run into great danger of encountering them in the mouth, as we cannot determine what our enemies intend: So it was then with unanimous

--- CHUNK 4 ---
still to be before Goa, as long as no certain news of their departure has been received; the defensive fleet could well avoid them, but would then betake itself again before Goa or come down along the Malabar Coast; whereby we, from Surat on the 14th of March in the year 1693, would run into great danger of encountering them in the mouth, as we cannot determine what our enemies intend: So it was then with unanimous voices deemed good to send the Equipment Master Leendert Blanckert with a swift rowing and sailing vessel to Cannanore to be dispatched with a letter to the chief officer Sir van der Duijn, whose copy is attached hereto, so that he would inform us what news he had of the French; Blanckert being charged with a piece of calico to ascertain from the English friends what they might know of the French, and especially, if he should discover any French ships on the way, to return with all speed to give us notice thereof, so that we might secure the Company's people, ship, and goods for the best and bring them into safety, as Your Excellency in the Copy Resolution attached hereto, remaining to be further considered, would be able to see, to which I conduct myself humbly, whereby it may also appear on the 30th of June 1693 by the Yacht Gaasperdam from Coromandel, from Surat on the 14th of March in the year 1693, that we (upon the departure of the French) shall continue our journey under God's gracious blessing and guidance; being we are strengthened against all unforeseen contingencies with a sergeant, corporal, and 12 soldiers, with the intention of today or tomorrow, as soon as the weather and wind permit, to weigh our anchor, what further stands to follow here I shall humbly report to Your Excellency at the next opportunity. Whereby &c. (signed below) Most Noble, Highly Commanding

On the 30th of June 1693, per the year Gaasperdam from Coromandel. From Surat on the 14th of March in the year 1693, we can, then we (upon the departure of the French) shall continue our journey under God's gracious blessing and guidance; being we are strengthened against all unforeseen accidents with a sergeant, corporal, and 12 soldiers, with the intention of departing today or tomorrow very early, as the weather and wind permit, to weigh our anchor, what further stands to follow here shall I humbly report to Your High Excellencies at a later opportunity. With which &c. (undersigned) Well Esteemed, High Commanding Lords; Your Excellencies' high esteemed, obedient and faithful servant (was signed) Louis de Keyser (in margin) Cochin on the 14th of March in the year 1693. — Batavia. To His Excellency the Lord and Master Willem van Outhoorn, Governor General, and the Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Netherlands India. Noble, Earnest, highly esteemed, valiant, wise, foreseeing, most generous Lords. — received at Batavia from Surat on the 23rd of March in the year 1693. — Well Esteemed High Commanding Lords. Herewith goes my youngest [letter] to Your High Excellencies of the 14th of this month, left here in the hands of the Esteemed Administrator Abraham Vink to be conveyed to Your High Excellencies at a more convenient time, to which I humbly attend, by this [letter] may Your High Excellencies be pleased to note that we on the 15th in the morning have weighed anchor to continue our journey to Surat, with which on the 19th after midday we had not progressed further than to before Caloor, lying between Pattani and Kalikout, doing our best to reach before Cananor, according to the resolution taken in this place on the 13th of this month: thus sailing onward, there appeared to us on the 19th after midday the Cochin Equipment Master with a letter sent ahead to Cananor, from where he brought me back a letter from the Lord Commander Isaac

--- CHUNK 2 ---
to continue, with which on the 19th after midday we had not progressed further than to before Caloor, lying between Pattani and Kalikout, doing our best to reach before Cananor, according to the resolution taken in this place on the 13th of this month: thus sailing onward, there appeared to us on the 19th after midday the Cochin Equipment Master with a letter sent ahead to Cananor, from where he brought me back a letter from the Lord Commander Isaac van Dielen, and the council on the fleet, anchored lying north of Montedeili, and dated the 17th of this month, of which the copy is in our resolution from Surat on the 23rd of March in the year 1693, attached on the 19th of this month. In reading and reflecting upon the contents thereof, I was greatly concerned about the withdrawal of the four French ships from Goa to between Barcelore and Carrewaer, and their cruising there in order to lie in wait for some prize, for the skipper and steersmen of Adrichem, making calculations regarding the crossing of the French to go around the Maldives to continue their journey to the Coast of Coromandel or their Comptoir Pondicherry, judged unanimously that this undertaking would come to nothing if they did not pick it up again beyond Wingurla to cross from there, therefore I regarded this crossing as a provocation of the French to entangle us and other their enemies thereby, and to see some chance. And I found it advisable to convene the ship's council, strengthened with the Cochin Equipment Master, to deliberate together and to consider what best should be done and to the greatest service of the Esteemed Company, taking in hand whether to continue on to Mangalore to be able to reach the fleet, which could not be done without the utmost from Surat on the 23rd of March in the year 1693, danger

--- CHUNK 3 ---
to entangle us and other their enemies thereby, and to see some chance. And I found it advisable to convene the ship's council, strengthened with the Cochin Equipment Master, to deliberate together and to consider what best should be done and to the greatest service of the Esteemed Company, taking in hand whether to continue on to Mangalore to be able to reach the fleet, which could not be done without the utmost from Surat on the 23rd of March in the year 1693, danger to run, could be accomplished, or to push it back again to Cochin, to keep our Company's ship and goods outside the peril of falling into the hands of enemies; so it is with unanimous voices judged best to set the ship back to Cochin at once, to unload it there, and to bring it into the river; and so that the Lord Commander Isaac van Dielen and the council on the fleet could be quickly informed of our deliberations, we have at once dispatched a letter to His Excellency and the council to Cananor, to be sent forward to the fleet as quickly as possible, of which the copy goes herewith, as likewise the copy of our drawn resolution. Thus have we pushed it back to Cochin, and arrived there on the 21st in the morning in good order, and are now busy unloading the ship and then bringing it into the river for safekeeping. Although the Lord Commander I. van Dielen and the council on the fleet make no mention of difficulties in their letter to me, and only say from Surat on the 23rd of March in the year 1693, that they will remain in expectation all hours to meet us and to hasten our arrival; so it appears His Excellency was inwardly of a quite different opinion and not a little concerned about us, as can be seen from

--- CHUNK 4 ---
Although the Lord Commander I. van Dielen and the council on the fleet make no mention of difficulties in their letter to me, and only say from Surat on the 23rd of March in the year 1693, that they will remain in expectation all hours to meet us and to hasten our arrival; so it appears His Excellency was inwardly of a quite different opinion and not a little concerned about us, as can be seen from the extract drawn from His Excellency's letter to the council of Cochin on the 15th of this month, herewith attached in copy, as likewise the copy of the little letter from the political council of Cochin to me on the 18th of this month for the guidance of the aforementioned extract, which was indeed sent after us; but the vessel escaped us, to which I humbly attend. It has weighed heavily upon me not to be able to continue our journey to Surat, and to have to retreat before we had seen enemies, but considering that it would then be too late to want to place the Company's ship and goods in safety, and how little advantage was to be expected from a courageous resistance; I have thought it better for the future and to meet the impending storm from the foreseeing fear to strike sail in time, than with an irresponsible recklessness from Surat on the 23rd of March in the year 1693, to place the Company's people, ship, and goods so apparently in the balance, without the Esteemed Company being able to draw any considerable service from it; moreover I have thought that it was better for the service of the Esteemed Company that the ships in the fleet destined for Surat could still complete their journey, than the same to wait with us and lose more time, where the monsoon has already progressed so far

--- CHUNK 5 ---
to place the Company's people, ship, and goods so apparently in the balance, without the Esteemed Company being able to draw any considerable service from it; moreover I have thought that it was better for the service of the Esteemed Company that the ships in the fleet destined for Surat could still complete their journey, than the same to wait with us and lose more time, where the monsoon has already progressed so far that it is to be feared whether they will be able to complete the journey comfortably, therefore I trust and hope that Your High Excellencies will regard my considerations as well-founded, and will take pleasure in our drawn resolution and return to Cochin, which to be able to understand at an opportunity will bring me great satisfaction, whereas I would on the contrary have reason to be grieved to the utmost if in these perilous matters I had undertaken anything contrary to Your High Excellencies' wise deliberation and opinions. With which &c. (undersigned) Your Excellencies' high esteemed, obedient and humble servant (was signed) L. de Keyser (in margin) Cochin on the 23rd of March 1693. —

From Surat on the 15th of April in the year 1693. — Most Esteemed, Highly Commanding Gentlemen. To the skipper of the fluyt High-Carspel I have handed over a packet of letters consigned to Your High Excellencies, in order to obtain good delivery via Tutucurin and Ceylon further on; in which two original letters from the 14th and 23rd of the past month are enclosed, as well as some other attachments, to which I conduct myself in all humility, but if the same should not yet have reached Your High Excellencies, I send herewith the copies of all those papers: After the departure of the aforementioned vessel, a letter from Cannanore has been brought here, signed by the chief and council there on the 29th of March, and consigned to me and the political council of Cochin, containing little of importance, yet the copy of the same goes herewith to Your High Excellencies for consideration, but the letter from the Mister Commander Isaac van Dielen, and the council

--- CHUNK 5 ---
should not yet have reached Your High Excellencies, I send herewith the copies of all those papers: After the departure of the aforementioned vessel, a letter from Cannanore has been brought here, signed by the chief and council there on the 29th of March, and consigned to me and the political council of Cochin, containing little of importance, yet the copy of the same goes herewith to Your High Excellencies for consideration, but the letter from the Mister Commander Isaac van Dielen, and the council on the fleet coming herewith, and signed in the ship the Great Fishery lying at anchor at Mangalore on the 25th of March 1693, was of greater weight to me, of which the copy is attached hereto, as is likewise the letter which I have had sent as a reply to the Mister Commander Isaac van Dielen, and the council, to which I conduct myself with all humility; Your High Excellencies will, if it please them, be able to observe that I have not overstepped myself in the same, but have restrained myself, the die being cast as it must remain lying and the past not to be undone; moreover, since the Company could draw no service from disputes and disagreements, but since I am obliged to give Your High Excellencies a strict account of my actions and omissions, I find myself compelled to add here some few considerations, which I had previously thought through, not knowing what answer the Mister Commander Isaac van Dielen would deign to give us to our writing. First of all, I cannot well reconcile myself to the fact that the aforementioned Mister Commander I. van Dielen in his Excellency's writing on the 15th of March to the political council at Cochin uses these words: the only thing From Surat on the 15th of April in the year 1693. that concerns us is the delay of the fluyt ship Adrichem

--- CHUNK 1 ---
have not known what answer the esteemed Commander Isaac van Dielen would be pleased to apply to our writings, in the first place; and I cannot well reconcile myself to the fact that the aforementioned esteemed Commander I. van Dielen in his Excellency's letter of the 15th of March to the political council at Cochin uses these words. From Surat on the 15th of April, Anno 1693. The only thing that concerns us is the falling behind of the fluyt ship Adrichem with the esteemed Surat's director Keyser, for it could happen that the enemies, catching sight of us, running seaward and southward, would meet the same, which would be for both the Company as well as his Excellency a lamentable occurrence, which God Almighty graciously prevent. And in the letter signed by his Excellency and the council in the ship the Great Fishery, lying at anchor north of Monte Deli, on the 17th of March 1693, not the least difficulty was mentioned, and only said, which following we shall remain in expectation to meet you at all hours, and thereafter, as if the French enemies were certainly gone, or if they would immediately choose the sea out of fear; while they for themselves assume along this Coast of India otherwise to encounter the fleet, which they know from Batavia has been sent out to seek them, for which reason it is very apparent that as soon as they catch sight of the present naval force in Surat on the 15th of April, Anno 1693, they will immediately scout for the others, and will not stand with us, but will hasten their intended voyage through open sea. On the contrary, I have firmly imagined myself, and still am (with the approval of the esteemed Commander I. van Dielen, and reserving his Excellency's better judgment) of the same opinion, that the French enemies (whom one knows well enough

--- CHUNK 2 ---
that as soon as they catch sight of the present naval force in Surat on the 15th of April, Anno 1693, they will immediately scout for the others, and will not stand with us, but will hasten their intended voyage through open sea. On the contrary, I have firmly imagined myself, and still am (with the approval of the esteemed Commander I. van Dielen, and reserving his Excellency's better judgment) of the same opinion, that the French enemies (whom one knows well enough that they spare no money to obtain good intelligence of matters to which they apply themselves) were well informed, from what ships the fleet consisted, which came sailing northward, without needing to imagine that it was the armada from Batavia—it being so much their concern to obtain good and certain information from the same, this not only, but also that it did not remain hidden from them that Adrichem, having arrived here, had only steered northward, upon which they then all the more boldly and confidently (the fleet going seaward, evading and passing by) could venture a chance in hope of good plunder. I believe that my thoughts are grounded in reason, there being in Surat on the 15th and April, Anno 1693, a full abundance of ill-willed Roman-minded spiritual and other people ill-disposed toward the Company, who would think to do God a service thereby, beyond the expectation of a rich reward. On the other hand, I cannot pass by without addressing something from the letter of the esteemed Commander I. van Dielen and the council signed in the ship the Great Fishery, lying at anchor at Mangalore on the 25th of March 1693, for my further and necessary justification. To not extend this letter much, I shall humbly defer to the
